accuracy.evidence: The steps and words follow the England KS1 programme of study for writing composition (plan or say out loud what they will write, write it down, reread to check it makes sense, make simple revisions, proofread for errors in spelling, grammar and punctuation) and the topic's own vocabulary list. Revise is used for improving words and ideas and edit or proofread for surface errors, matching the plan, draft, revise and edit stages in the EEF literacy guidance. Instructions, recount and narrative match standard KS1 genre teaching.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: confusing revising with editing (prediction 3, the fix-a-full-stop decoy chip in the revise scene, the visual sorter and the revise/edit feedback in the challenge), thinking a draft must be neat or that writing is done after the draft (step 1 text and mastery m8), recount versus made-up story (purpose matcher and m5/m7), and audience versus purpose (challenge feedback).

lab_distinct.evidence: Built for this topic: a four-tile ordering path for plan, draft, revise and edit, a first-next-last story planner, a revise scene where tapping detail chips grows the sentence and changes the dog picture, a word-tile sentence where tapping the three mistakes edits it, and a writing-job matcher. It shares no mechanics with flagcraft (register and cohesion), and the distinctness gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step needs the learner to do the step it names: wrong tiles shake back with 'Not yet, Revise comes after Draft', the plan has to be put in time order, the revise task only counts real detail words while the editing chip explains why it is not revising, editing only counts the capital, spelling and full stop, and each writing job must be matched to its kind.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each answered by the task that follows: what writers do first (the ordering path), whether adding 'fluffy' is revising or editing (the detail chips) and whether fixing a capital letter is editing (the mistake taps). The reveal repeats the child's own choice with spot on or the correct word.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Ten scenario cards, each with three word choices. A wrong revise/edit pick gets the contrast line 'Revise makes it better. Edit fixes mistakes.', and an audience or purpose slip gets the who/why line. Any other slip gets the definitions of both the chosen word and the right word. The canvas then shows the right word with its meaning, and a star count builds.

readability.evidence: Child text uses very short sentences and everyday words (first go, messy, fix, big, fluffy), and the family readability gate passed for both kid and adult text. Lab instructions are one or two short sentences, and every tile shows an emoji picture next to its word for children who are still learning to read.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph names and applies one or more of the process words with an example (the kite story, 'I saw a dog', the birthday card). The content gate found no banned filler words, and the adult text goes straight to the lab's actions, the common mistakes and a concrete routine to use at home.

mobile.evidence: Uses the young class for 56px buttons. Checked on iPhone 13: the four step tiles go into a 2x2 grid, story and job cards are about a third of the width with big emoji, the sentence tiles fit in one row, and sub-labels are dropped when they would not fit. Every canvas target has a full-size button below.

accessibility.evidence: axe passes in both themes on desktop and iPhone. Every canvas tap has a labelled button. The canvas aria-label reports what is placed, the current sentence or the current writing job, and the challenge uses real buttons with polite live feedback. Feedback does not rely on colour alone: a tick, the words and the changed sentence all show it.
